title: Top N and bottom N
summary_md: Pick the highest or lowest N rows overall, per group, after aggregation, or the Nth value, and know exactly what happens on ties and NULLs.

sections.heading: Top N overall
sections.body_md:
- Sort by the measure, then cut: `ORDER BY measure DESC` + a row limiter.
- MySQL: `LIMIT n [OFFSET skip]`. SQL Server: `TOP (n)`, or `OFFSET skip ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY` (needs `ORDER BY`).
- Always add a tiebreaker column (an id). Without it, which tied row survives the cut is arbitrary.
- `LIMIT` / `TOP` return exactly N rows, so a tie at the boundary is cut. If ties must stay, use `RANK` (see the last section).
- NULL counts as the smallest value in both MySQL and SQL Server: `DESC` puts NULL last, `ASC` puts NULL first.

syntax.mysql: SELECT cols FROM t [WHERE ...] ORDER BY measure DESC, tiebreak LIMIT n [OFFSET skip]
syntax.tsql:
SELECT TOP (n) cols FROM t ORDER BY measure DESC, tiebreak
-- or, for paging:
SELECT cols FROM t ORDER BY measure DESC, tiebreak OFFSET skip ROWS FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY

args.name: measure DESC
args.meaning: The column that defines 'top'. DESC = biggest first.

args.name: tiebreak
args.meaning: Second sort key (usually the primary key) so the result is deterministic.

args.name: LIMIT n / TOP (n) / FETCH NEXT n
OFFSET skip
args.meaning: How many rows to skip first. Page k of size n skips (k-1)*n.

examples.title: Three highest salaries
examples.explain_md: Ben and Cara tie at 150000; the `emp_id` tiebreaker decides Ben comes first. The NULL salary sorts last under DESC, so it never shows up here.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id LIMIT 3;
examples.tsql: SELECT TOP (3) name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id;

examples.title: Three newest hires
examples.explain_md: Same pattern on a date column: latest date = biggest value.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, hire_date FROM employees ORDER BY hire_date DESC, emp_id LIMIT 3;
examples.tsql: SELECT TOP (3) name, hire_date FROM employees ORDER BY hire_date DESC, emp_id;

examples.title: Page 2 of the salary ranking (rows 4-6)
examples.explain_md: Skip the first 3, take the next 3. In SQL Server `FETCH` is only legal after `OFFSET`, and both need `ORDER BY`.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id OFFSET 3 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY;

pitfalls_md: `TOP` / `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns arbitrary rows, not the 'first' rows.
`OFFSET` paging gets slower the deeper you go and shifts if rows are inserted between pages.

sections.heading: Top N per group: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
sections.body_md:
- Number the rows inside each group, then keep the rows whose number is `<= N`. A window function cannot go in `WHERE`, so wrap it in a CTE or subquery.
- Which function you number with decides what happens on ties:
  - `ROW_NUMBER()`: 1,2,3,4. Never ties, so you get exactly N rows per group (tiebreaker decides who).
  - `RANK()`: 1,2,2,4. Ties share a rank and the next rank is skipped. Keeps all tied rows, so a group can return more than N.
  - `DENSE_RANK()`: 1,2,2,3. Ties share a rank, no gap. `<= N` returns the top N distinct values.
- Neither MySQL nor SQL Server has `QUALIFY`; the CTE-then-filter shape is the only way.

syntax.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT cols, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY measure DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM t
)
SELECT cols FROM r WHERE rn <= N
syntax.tsql: -- identical; RANK() and DENSE_RANK() drop in for ROW_NUMBER()

args.name: PARTITION BY grp
args.meaning: Restarts the numbering for each group (dept, region, user...).

args.name: ORDER BY measure DESC
args.meaning: Defines who is 'top' inside the group.

args.name: id (tiebreak)
args.meaning: Needed with ROW_NUMBER so equal measures get a stable order. Pointless with RANK/DENSE_RANK.

args.name: rn <= N
args.meaning: The cut. Applied in the outer query because windows cannot be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE.

examples.title: All three functions on the same data
examples.explain_md: Engineering: Ben and Cara tie at 150000. ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2; RANK gives 1,1 then jumps to 3 for Dev; DENSE_RANK gives 1,1 then 2. Sales shows the same with Gus/Hal.
examples.mysql:
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC, emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC, emp_id;

examples.title: Top 2 earners per department: exactly 2 (ROW_NUMBER)
examples.explain_md: Exactly two rows for every department that has two or more people. Sales keeps Gus and drops Hal only because of the `emp_id` tiebreak; an arbitrary pick between equals.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) AS rn
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, rn
FROM r
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY dept, rn;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) AS rn
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, rn
FROM r
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY dept, rn;

examples.title: Top 2 per department, keep ties (RANK)
examples.explain_md: Sales now returns three people: Fay is rank 1, Gus and Hal share rank 2. Engineering returns Ben and Cara (both rank 1), and Dev (rank 3) is out.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, rnk
FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY dept, rnk, name;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, rnk
FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY dept, rnk, name;

examples.title: Top 2 distinct salary levels per department (DENSE_RANK)
examples.explain_md: Engineering returns Ben, Cara and Dev: the two highest *salary levels* are 150000 and 120000, and the tie at 150000 counts as one level.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, drnk
FROM r
WHERE drnk <= 2
ORDER BY dept, drnk, name;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, drnk
FROM r
WHERE drnk <= 2
ORDER BY dept, drnk, name;

pitfalls_md: Filtering on a window alias in the same SELECT's `WHERE` is an error. Compute it in a CTE/subquery and filter outside.
A NULL measure under `DESC` ranks last, but it still takes a slot if the group is small (Marketing would show Jon with a NULL salary). Filter NULLs first if they are not real data.
ROW_NUMBER without a tiebreaker is non-deterministic on ties: the same query can return different people on different runs.

sections.heading: Bottom N (and the NULL trap)
sections.body_md:
- Bottom N = flip the sort to `ASC`. Same patterns: `LIMIT`/`TOP` overall, `ROW_NUMBER`/`RANK` per group with `ORDER BY measure ASC`.
- NULL is the smallest value in MySQL and SQL Server, so under `ASC` NULLs come first and steal the 'lowest' slots.
- Decide what NULL means: not real data (filter with `WHERE measure IS NOT NULL`) or a value you want ranked last (sort on `CASE WHEN measure IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, measure`).
- `NULLS LAST` is not available in either MySQL or SQL Server; the `CASE` sort key is the portable form.

examples.title: Three lowest salaries (NULL steals the first slot)
examples.explain_md: Jon is a contractor with NULL salary. Ascending, NULL sorts first, so 'lowest' returns a person with no salary at all.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary, emp_id LIMIT 3;
examples.tsql: SELECT TOP (3) name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary, emp_id;

examples.title: Three lowest salaries, NULLs removed
examples.explain_md: Gus and Hal tie at 80000 and Ivy is next at 90000. If a fourth row were wanted, Hal's tie with Gus would matter again.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary, emp_id LIMIT 3;
examples.tsql: SELECT TOP (3) name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary, emp_id;

examples.title: Keep NULL rows but sort them last
examples.explain_md: The `CASE` key is 0 for real values and 1 for NULL, so NULLs fall to the end of an ascending sort. Here it gives the same three people as filtering.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, salary, emp_id LIMIT 3;
examples.tsql: SELECT TOP (3) name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, salary, emp_id;

examples.title: Lowest-paid employee per department
examples.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER ascending, keep rn = 1. Departments with one person (Exec) return that person; Marketing returns Ivy because Jon's NULL was filtered out first.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary, emp_id) AS rn
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM r
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dept;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary, emp_id) AS rn
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM r
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dept;

pitfalls_md: Forgetting the NULL filter on bottom-N is the classic bug: the 'lowest' row is the one with no value.
Do not fake ASC by negating the column; just write `ASC`.

sections.heading: Nth highest value
sections.body_md:
- 'Second highest salary' almost always means the second highest *distinct* value, so ties must collapse: `DENSE_RANK` or `SELECT DISTINCT`.
- `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC) = n`: the portable, per-group-friendly answer. Returns zero rows if there is no nth value.
- `ORDER BY x DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1` (MySQL) / `OFFSET n-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY` (SQL Server) on a `SELECT DISTINCT` list: works, but zero rows again if missing.
- Wrap either in a scalar subquery, `SELECT (subquery) AS nth`, and a missing nth value becomes a single-row NULL. That is what interviewers usually want.
- Max trick for n = 2: `MAX(x) WHERE x < (SELECT MAX(x))`. Naturally NULL when missing; does not scale to bigger n.

args.name: DISTINCT x
args.meaning: Collapses ties so each value counts once.

args.name: ORDER BY x DESC
args.meaning: Largest first. Required for OFFSET/FETCH in SQL Server.

args.name: n-1
args.meaning: Rows to skip: for the 3rd highest skip 2.

args.name: outer SELECT (...)
args.meaning: Scalar subquery: no row becomes NULL instead of an empty result.

examples.title: 3rd highest salary with DENSE_RANK
examples.explain_md: Distinct non-NULL salaries are 250000, 150000, 120000, ... so the 3rd highest is 120000. `DISTINCT` is needed because several rows can share a rank.
examples.mysql:
SELECT DISTINCT salary AS third_highest
FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
) x
WHERE drnk = 3;
examples.tsql:
SELECT DISTINCT salary AS third_highest
FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
) x
WHERE drnk = 3;

examples.title: OFFSET form, with NULL when there is no nth value
examples.explain_md: There are only 7 distinct salaries, so the 8th highest does not exist. The scalar-subquery wrapper turns the empty result into NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT
  (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
   ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2) AS third_highest,
  (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
   ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 7) AS eighth_highest;
examples.tsql:
SELECT
  (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
   ORDER BY salary DESC OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY) AS third_highest,
  (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
   ORDER BY salary DESC OFFSET 7 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY) AS eighth_highest;

examples.title: 2nd highest with the MAX trick
examples.explain_md: Take the biggest value that is smaller than the overall biggest. `MAX` over zero rows is NULL, so a missing value needs no wrapper.
examples.mysql: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
examples.tsql: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

examples.title: 2nd highest salary per department (NULL where missing)
examples.explain_md: Rank inside each department, then pick rank 2 with `MAX(CASE ...)`. Groups with fewer than two distinct salaries (Exec, Marketing) still appear, with NULL.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT e.dept,
       MAX(CASE WHEN r.drnk = 2 THEN r.salary END) AS second_highest
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM employees) e
LEFT JOIN r ON r.dept = e.dept
GROUP BY e.dept
ORDER BY e.dept;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT e.dept,
       MAX(CASE WHEN r.drnk = 2 THEN r.salary END) AS second_highest
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM employees) e
LEFT JOIN r ON r.dept = e.dept
GROUP BY e.dept
ORDER BY e.dept;

pitfalls_md: `LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` without `DISTINCT` returns the 2nd *row*: with Ben and Cara tied at 150000 it returns 150000, the same as the highest tie, not the 2nd highest value.
`DENSE_RANK` = nth distinct value; `ROW_NUMBER` = nth row; `RANK` skips numbers after a tie and may never equal n. Say which one you mean.
MySQL's `LIMIT` does not accept an expression like `n-1`; compute the number first or hard-code it.

sections.heading: Top N after aggregation
sections.body_md:
- Two stages: `GROUP BY` to get one row per entity with its total, then rank/limit those totals.
- Overall top N entities: aggregate, `ORDER BY total DESC, tiebreak`, `LIMIT`/`TOP`.
- Top N entities per group: aggregate in a CTE, then `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY total DESC)` in a second step and filter.
- Filter rows that should not count (cancelled, refunded) in the inner `WHERE`, before totals are computed.

examples.title: Top 2 cities by completed spend
examples.explain_md: Join, filter to completed orders, sum per city, then cut to 2. Austin sums several customers' completed orders. NULL city (Olga) is excluded here.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spend
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed' AND c.city IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY total_spend DESC, c.city
LIMIT 2;
examples.tsql:
SELECT TOP (2) c.city, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spend
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed' AND c.city IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY total_spend DESC, c.city;

examples.title: Biggest-spending customer in each month
examples.explain_md: Stage 1 totals completed spend per customer per month. Stage 2 ranks inside each month and keeps rank 1. RANK keeps a tie if two customers spend the same.
examples.mysql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT MONTH(order_date) AS mo, customer_id, SUM(amount) AS spend
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY MONTH(order_date), customer_id
), ranked AS (
  SELECT mo, customer_id, spend,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mo ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rnk
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT mo, customer_id, spend
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY mo, customer_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT MONTH(order_date) AS mo, customer_id, SUM(amount) AS spend
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY MONTH(order_date), customer_id
), ranked AS (
  SELECT mo, customer_id, spend,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mo ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rnk
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT mo, customer_id, spend
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY mo, customer_id;

examples.title: Window over an aggregate in one SELECT
examples.explain_md: A window function runs after `GROUP BY`, so it can rank the sums directly: `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(...) DESC)`. You still need an outer query to filter on the rank.
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id, total_spend, rnk
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id,
         SUM(amount) AS total_spend,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY customer_id
) t
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id, total_spend, rnk
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id,
         SUM(amount) AS total_spend,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY customer_id
) t
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, customer_id;

pitfalls_md: Putting the status filter in the outer query instead of the inner one ranks cancelled money too.
`GROUP BY MONTH(order_date)` merges the same month of different years; group by year and month (or a month-start date) on multi-year data.

sections.heading: Keeping ties: TOP ... WITH TIES
sections.body_md:
- SQL Server has a built-in: `SELECT TOP (n) WITH TIES ... ORDER BY measure DESC` returns the top n rows plus every row tied with the last one.
- It needs `ORDER BY`, cannot be combined with `OFFSET`, and ties are judged on the full `ORDER BY` list.
- MySQL has no equivalent. The portable form is `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY measure DESC) <= n`, which is what the examples below run (the in-browser engine cannot execute `WITH TIES`).
- Rule of thumb: `TOP n WITH TIES` is about the same as `RANK() <= n`.

syntax.mysql:
-- no WITH TIES in MySQL; use:
WITH r AS (SELECT cols, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY measure DESC) AS rnk FROM t)
SELECT cols FROM r WHERE rnk <= n
syntax.tsql: SELECT TOP (n) WITH TIES cols FROM t ORDER BY measure DESC

args.name: TOP (n) WITH TIES
args.meaning: Keep n rows plus all rows equal to the n-th row on the ORDER BY key.

args.name: RANK() <= n
args.meaning: Portable equivalent: ties share a rank, so every tied row passes the filter.

examples.title: Top 3 salaries, ties kept
examples.explain_md: Ana is rank 1, Ben and Cara share rank 2, Dev is rank 4. `rnk <= 3` returns Ana, Ben, Cara; Dev (4th place) is excluded.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT name, salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT name, salary, rnk
FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, name;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT name, salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT name, salary, rnk
FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, name;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server shortcut for this query (not run in the browser): `SELECT TOP (3) WITH TIES name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary DESC;`. TOP counts rows by position, then extends over rows equal to the last one, so here it also returns Ana, Ben, Cara.

examples.title: Top 3 completed order amounts, ties kept
examples.explain_md: Two orders are exactly 120.00. The amounts are 300, 200, 120, 120: asking for the top 3 returns four rows because rank 3 is shared.
examples.mysql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT order_id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rnk
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT order_id, amount, rnk
FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, order_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT order_id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rnk
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT order_id, amount, rnk
FROM r
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, order_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server shortcut (not run in the browser): `SELECT TOP (3) WITH TIES order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' ORDER BY amount DESC;` returns the same four rows.

pitfalls_md: `TOP (n) WITH TIES` without `ORDER BY` is a syntax error.
Ties are evaluated on every column in the `ORDER BY`, so adding an id tiebreaker removes the ties and turns it back into a plain TOP.
